details:
**Aristophanes' myth of the split humans**
The comic playwright Aristophanes claims humans were once round, double creatures with four arms, four legs, and two faces, until Zeus cut them in half for their arrogance. Love is the longing of each half to find its "other half," and the myth also explains why some people love the same sex and others the opposite sex.

**Diotima of Mantinea**
A priestess, possibly fictional, whose teachings on love Socrates recounts as the centerpiece of the dialogue. She is the only female voice in the work, and Socrates presents her as the person who taught him about Eros.

**The ladder of love**
Diotima's account of how a lover climbs step by step from loving one beautiful body, to all beautiful bodies, to beautiful souls, laws and institutions, and knowledge, until finally seeing Beauty itself, the eternal Form of beauty. This ascent is the dialogue's most famous philosophical idea.

**Alcibiades' drunken speech about Socrates**
Near the end, the Athenian politician Alcibiades bursts in drunk and praises Socrates instead of love. He describes how he tried and failed to seduce Socrates, who was unmoved by physical pleasure, and he recalls Socrates' toughness on military campaign.

**Silenus statues and Marsyas**
Alcibiades compares Socrates to hollow statues of the ugly satyr Silenus that open to reveal little images of the gods inside: ugly on the outside, divine within. He also calls Socrates a more wonderful performer than the satyr Marsyas, because Socrates enchants people with words alone instead of the flute.

**Aristophanes' hiccups and Eryximachus**
Aristophanes gets hiccups when his turn comes, so the doctor Eryximachus speaks in his place and suggests cures such as holding his breath, gargling, or sneezing. Eryximachus says love operates throughout nature as a harmony or agreement of opposites, as in medicine and music. John Adams later joked that all he learned from Plato's Symposium was a cure for the hiccups.

**A drinking party at Agathon's house**
The title means "drinking party." The tragic poet Agathon hosts the gathering to celebrate his first victory in the tragedy competition, and the guests agree to drink moderately and each give a speech in praise of Eros, the god of love.

**Apollodorus and Aristodemus (the frame story)**
The dialogue is narrated by Apollodorus, who tells an unnamed friend about the party years afterward. He heard about it from Aristodemus, a follower of Socrates who was actually there.

**Pausanias' Heavenly and Common love**
Pausanias argues there are two Aphrodites and so two kinds of love. "Common" (Pandemian) love comes from the Aphrodite born of Zeus and Dione and seeks bodies. "Heavenly" (Uranian) love comes from the Aphrodite born of Uranus alone, with no mother, and seeks souls and virtue. He defends the lover's willing "slavery for the sake of virtue" and discusses how Athenian law and custom treat love.

**Phaedrus and Achilles and Patroclus**
Phaedrus gives the first speech, calling Eros the oldest of the gods. He argues love makes people brave and willing to die for one another, and says an army of lovers would be unbeatable, citing Achilles avenging Patroclus and Alcestis dying for her husband.

**Love as the child of Resource and Poverty**
Diotima says Eros is not a god but a spirit between gods and mortals, born to Poros (Resource) and Penia (Poverty). Love is therefore always needy but always resourceful, and it seeks the beauty and wisdom it lacks. This is why love is linked to philosophy, the love of wisdom.

**Agathon's speech**
The host praises Eros himself as the youngest, most beautiful, and most delicate of the gods, in a polished, poetic speech. Socrates then questions him and gets him to admit that love desires beauty and so must lack it.

**Socrates' sandals and trance on the porch**
At the start, Aristodemus meets Socrates freshly bathed and wearing fancy sandals, unusual for him, as he heads to the party. On the way Socrates falls into thought and stands still on a neighbor's porch for a long time, arriving late.

**Xenophon's Symposium**
Xenophon also wrote a Symposium starring Socrates. It is set at a party given by the wealthy Callias, who is in love with the young athlete Autolycus.

**Kierkegaard's "In Vino Veritas"**
The first section of Kierkegaard's Stages on Life's Way, "In Vino Veritas," imitates Plato's Symposium. In it several characters give speeches about love and women at a banquet.
